extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers and literary critics (general readership interested in composition and criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical maxims for composing, revising, and judging imaginative works (essayistic guidance aimed at young writers and critics). Emphasises fidelity to nature, careful revision, judicious reading, and cautions about critical vanity and affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The chief business of art is to copy nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should imitate or copy nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a central position Minim lays down; used to evaluate whether writers attend to natural behavior and plausibility in characters and events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius and judgement trade off; perfect writer not to be expected
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect writer is not to be expected, because genius decays as judgment increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies humility in expectations for authors and suggests that maturity brings judgment that may lessen raw genius; used as a tempering principle in evaluating authors' strengths and weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: The great art is the art of blotting
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writing depends crucially on the ability to erase and revise (blotting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages editing and pruning as a major element of craft: quality arises from cutting away excess as much as from initial inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay publication: 'every piece should be kept nine years'
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the rule of Horace invoked by Minim, every piece should be kept nine years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conservative rule of thumb advising distance/time before final judgment or publication to avoid premature enthusiasm and to allow perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: All great authors have beauties and defects
rubrics_metrics.description: A universal position: all writers possess both merits and faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes balanced criticism—avoid absolute condemnation or idolatry; critique should acknowledge mixed qualities rather than demand perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance learning and nature (Shakespeare vs. Jonson model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare committed wholly to the impulse of nature and 'wanted that correctness which learning would have given him'; Jonson trusted to learning but did not cast his eyes on nature sufficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion: the best writing balances natural impulse and learned correctness; faults arise from excess of either tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about rhyming tragedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhyming tragedies are often unnatural; sense is sacrificed to sound when one line always ends like another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefers blank verse or diversified pauses; allows rhyme only conditionally (see separate entry). Use this to judge appropriateness of rhyme to dramatic seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme acceptable only with varied line-breaking and diversified pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhyme may sometimes be borne, if the lines be often broken, and the pauses judiciously diversified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conditional acceptance: rhythmic/structural variety can mitigate the awkwardness of rhyme in longer or serious pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: business is the soul; beware of excessive predominance of love
rubrics_metrics.description: In tragedy business is the soul, and yet sometimes love predominates too much upon the modern stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for dramatic content: maintain a central dramatic purpose (business); avoid letting romantic intrigue overwhelm substantive action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match sound to sense: 'the sound an echo to the sense'
rubrics_metrics.description: Versification should, where possible, make the sound echo the meaning (examples given from Hudibras).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Onomatopoeic, prosodic effects and careful placement of sounds can reinforce meaning and produce delight; critics should look for these accommodations of sound to sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of numbers and deliberate ruggedness (Milton's model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetual variation of numbers (meter) gratifies the ear; rugged or unmusical lines may temper melodious luxury and express particular things by cadence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhythmic variation and occasional roughness intentionally to sustain attention and to fit the matter; avoid monotonous melody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not trust authorial name; judge works on their own merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Minim is not so confident as to not catch new light from the name of the author, but generally spares those he cannot resist unless public opinion combines against them; he initially uses general terms until success is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against authorial bias: a prudent critic should withhold final judgment based solely on reputation and allow a work's reception to inform private praise or censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague epithets in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Minim uses favourite epithets like 'manly', 'dry', 'stiff', 'flimsy' even when he hasn't settled their meaning or read the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: critics should avoid relying on vague, fashionable labels without clear criteria or close reading; specificity is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pupil advice: read only the best authors and imitate their beauties, avoid their faults
rubrics_metrics.description: When advising a promising youth, advise him to read none but the best authors; when he finds one congenial, to study his beauties but avoid his faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructional prescription for study: selective, deep reading and conscious emulation tempered by critical avoidance of modeled faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider how your favourite author would think on the present occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: When sitting down to write, consider how your favourite author would think at the present time on the present occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A technique for learning style and approach—use as a thought experiment but do not lose one's own voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seize moments of inspiration but restrain imagination by nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Catch those moments when thoughts are expanded and genius exalted, but take care lest imagination hurry him beyond the bounds of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance spontaneity and discipline: write when inspiration flows, but ensure imagination remains plausible and grounded in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and measured reading: 'diligence the mother of success' and 'not to read more than he can digest'
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence is essential; do not read more than you can digest or confuse your mind by pursuing studies of contrary tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study habits: sustained effort and focused, assimilable reading produce better results than scattershot or excessive study across conflicting disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every man has his genius; write according to your natural gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man has his genius, and Cicero could never be a poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages authenticity: writers should recognize their natural strengths and not attempt forms utterly unsuited to their temper or talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics should be modest and prudent in pronouncements
rubrics_metrics.description: Minim is often inclined to censure fresh pretenders till success requires him to commend them; he uses general terms until the success of a composition is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice for critics: avoid overconfidence, be prepared to revise initial judgments, and resist the urge to domineer the conversation or impose arbitrary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional standard of taste is dangerous but proposed by some
rubrics_metrics.description: Minim forms a plan for an academy of criticism where every work of imagination may be read before it is printed and which shall authoritatively direct theatres what pieces to receive or reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation/criterion: while a tribunal of taste would enforce nicety and exclude works not conforming to rules, the essay treats this with irony—warning about institutional censorship and rigidity even while noting desire for a 'standard of taste'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'false delicacy' and ornamental affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Minim alternately deplores 'false delicacy' gaining ground and predicts the revival of the true sublime; warns against 'petty refinements and ornamental luxuriance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style guidance: seek noble simplicity over petty refinements; beware of mannered ornament that sacrifices force and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical arts are laudable only when they increase perspicuity and pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts of rhetoric and poetry—the regulation of figures, selection of words, modulation of periods—are useful while they advance perspicuity, and laudable while they increase pleasure, but easy to be refined by needless scrupulosity till they shall embarrass the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical techniques instrumentally: they should clarify and delight, not obscure or overrefine; avoid excessive scruple that obstructs communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not delay publication through scrupulosity; life is short, knowledge endless
rubrics_metrics.description: Let those whom nature and study have qualified to teach mankind tell us what they have learned while they are yet able to tell it, and trust their reputation only to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical admonition to scholars/authors: avoid perpetual polishing that prevents sharing knowledge; publish imperfectly rather than never, since endless revision can bury useful work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware vanity and performative criticism (the social performance of being a critic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minim's conduct—seeking applause, presiding in coffee-houses, influencing audiences with a clap or murmur—shows criticism as social performance and vanity more than service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-criterion: critics should self-scrutinize motives and avoid performative, vanity-driven habits; good criticism serves the work and public understanding rather than personal display.

rubrics_metrics.name: On the evolution of language and danger of affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Language progresses from rudeness to convenience to elegance and then to nicety; as civilization advances there is danger that care will too soon pass to affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging style, prize clarity and usefulness over excessive nicety; be skeptical of innovations that amount to mere ornament rather than communicative improvement.
